questions.q: What problem does a Python virtual environment solve?
options: It isolates each project's installed packages, avoiding version conflicts between projects sharing one global Python
It makes Python code execute faster
It automatically updates all your installed packages
It replaces the need to write a requirements.txt file
questions.explain: Without a venv, every project installs into the same global site-packages, so two projects needing different versions of the same library conflict. A venv gives each project its own isolated set.

questions.q: What command creates a new virtual environment named `.venv`?
options: pip create .venv
venv new .venv
python -m venv .venv
python install venv .venv
questions.explain: python -m venv <name> runs the built-in venv module, creating an isolated environment folder with its own Python interpreter and site-packages.

questions.q: Once a virtual environment is activated, what does `pip install requests` do?
options: Installs requests only into the active virtual environment, not system-wide
Installs requests into the system Python, bypassing the virtual environment
Only downloads the package without installing it
Installs requests into every virtual environment on the machine
questions.explain: With a virtual environment active, pip install (and pip in general) operates on that environment's isolated package set, leaving the system Python and other environments untouched.

questions.q: Why would you run `pip install requests==2.31.0` instead of just `pip install requests`?
options: The == syntax is required the first time any package is installed
It pins an exact version, guaranteeing reproducible installs instead of whatever version happens to be newest
It installs the package twice for redundancy
It uninstalls any existing version first automatically with no other effect
questions.explain: Pinning a version with == ensures everyone installing from the same instruction gets the identical version, rather than each person getting whatever the latest release happens to be at install time.

questions.q: A teammate says 'I installed the package, but my script still can't import it.' What's the most likely cause, based on this lesson?
options: Python itself is broken and needs reinstalling
The virtual environment was never activated (or a different one got activated), so the install and the running script are using different Python environments
pip only works on Linux
The package name must always match the import name exactly, with no exceptions
questions.explain: This is the classic venv mix-up: if the environment isn't active (or the wrong one is), pip install and your running script end up pointing at two different Python installations with two different sets of packages.
